origins.name: President's Scholar

origins.name: Poly, then night classes

startBand.note: How far a new career's four starting stats may sit from its origin's (origins[].stats): up to `default` either way, or the origin's own `startBand` for that stat. Drawn from the seed on a stream of its own, so the same seed starts the same career and nothing else in the run moves. The bands keep the origins apart where they are ranked: every scholar starts with more standing and reputation than any graduate, and every graduate more than any poly entrant (test/harness.test.js checks it).

endings.title: Prime Minister
endings.epitaph: You made it. The formula pays you twice the entry-grade minister's salary, and the formula was published, so nobody can say they were not told.

endings.title: Permanent Secretary
endings.epitaph: The top of the civil service. No street is named after you and none ever will be, which is rather the point.

endings.title: You Found Your Level
endings.epitaph: Four decades, give or take, and retirement savings that will comfortably outlast you. The pewter plate says "{player.full}, with appreciation". The scheme you designed in year nine is still running.

endings.title: The Tea Was Declined
endings.epitaph: The party asked you to stand for election, and you said no. You are not sure, even now, whether it was principle or nerve. Everyone who knows you thinks it was principle.

endings.title: Lost the Ward
endings.epitaph: Forty-eight point two percent. You shook every hand in that ward and it was not enough. The concession speech was the best speech you ever gave.

endings.title: Everything Surfaced
endings.epitaph: Everything you had kept quiet came out in one week, which was merciful in its way. The press conference was eleven minutes long, and the next morning's headline was "{player.formal} resigns".

endings.title: The Quiet Conversation
endings.epitaph: You were asked whether you had considered the private sector. No announcement was made. The email to your colleagues said only that {player.formal} "has moved on", and wished {player.them} well. Your pass stopped working on a Friday.

endings.title: Backbench Lifer
endings.epitaph: Never a portfolio. But at your last Meet-the-People Session there was a queue out the door, and half of them had come only to say "Thank you, {player.formal}".

endings.title: Never Quite Cabinet
endings.epitaph: You answered Members' questions in Parliament, from answers your old colleagues had drafted, and answered them well. Cabinet was always one reshuffle away.

endings.title: Retired, Honourably
endings.epitaph: You served. The service continued. Both of these facts are entirely unremarkable and that is the highest compliment the system can pay.

endings.title: The Consultancy
endings.epitaph: You now advise ministries on the problems you used to have. The decks are better designed than your memos were. They say the same things, and they cost $1.9 million.

endings.title: The Invitation Lapsed
endings.epitaph: The party read your file and decided the country could wait. You were never told which page. You have narrowed it down to three.

declassifiedFlags.label: The U-turn
declassifiedFlags.text: You defended a policy in the House. Two years later it was reversed, and you had the statement say plainly that it had been wrong. Hansard keeps both.

declassifiedFlags.label: The U-turn
declassifiedFlags.text: Your old replies went into the statement as "the position at the time". Hansard keeps the position, the time, and the day it changed.

declassifiedFlags.label: The U-turn

declassifiedFlags.label: The U-turn
declassifiedFlags.text: Your policy was not reversed: it was phased out over six months, at your suggestion. The minutes say so.

declassifiedFlags.label: The U-turn
declassifiedFlags.text: You argued to keep the policy, quoting your own replies in the House. The minutes say you "raised considerations".

declassifiedFlags.label: The U-turn
declassifiedFlags.text: You agreed the policy should go, quickly. Nobody mentioned your old replies, which was a courtesy.

declassifiedFlags.label: The U-turn
declassifiedFlags.text: Your replies to nine Parliamentary Questions on the policy are in Hansard, word for word. The policy was never reversed, so they are still the position, at the time.

declassifiedFlags.label: The bond

declassifiedFlags.label: The bond
declassifiedFlags.text: An eight-year bond in all: six years of service for the degree, two more for the master's, and one bank's offer to buy you out, declined along the way.

declassifiedFlags.label: The bond

Your integrity is intact, which took some doing.

competence.label: Competence
competence.about: Competence is how good you were at the work itself. Good work earned the good yearly grades that got you promoted, and a bigger bonus every year.

bands.text: Your Competence was high: your work was the best thing in your file, and your bonus was near the most it could be.
Your Competence was solid: good enough to do the job, but not good enough to win a promotion without help from your Standing and Reputation.
Your Competence was below par, so it pulled your grades down and kept your bonus small.
Your Competence was very low: it cost you grades and promotions, and it kept your bonus near the minimum.

standing.label: Standing
standing.about: Standing is how far the people above you trusted you: your bosses in the service, or the party leadership once you were in politics. Their trust helped your yearly grade, and the party only invites people to tea, its first quiet approach to a possible election candidate, once both their Standing and their Reputation are high enough.

bands.text: Your Standing was high enough for tea, and high enough to be considered when the party picks its next Prime Minister.
Your Standing was high enough for tea, as long as your Reputation was too.
Your Standing was too low for tea: the people above you did not trust you enough to put your name forward.
Your Standing was very low: the people above you did not trust you, and that held back your grades and kept you far from tea.

reputation.label: Reputation
reputation.about: Reputation is what the public thought of you. It decided how likely you were to win an election, and the party checks it, alongside Standing, before inviting anyone to tea.

bands.text: Your Reputation was high enough that, at an election, you could have run alone for a seat of your own, not just as one of a party team.
Your Reputation was respectable, but too low to run alone for a seat, so at an election you would have run as one of a party team.
Your Reputation was low. Outside work, almost nobody knew your name, and the party does not invite people nobody knows to tea.

integrity.label: Integrity
integrity.about: Integrity is what you did when nobody was checking. It never helped your grade or your promotions, but it decided most of what people said about you when you left.

bands.text: Your Integrity held: when the right thing cost you something, you usually paid.
Your Integrity bent now and then: you cut some corners, but not many.
Your Integrity gave way most of the time: whenever the right thing cost you something, you found a reason not to pay.

quiet.text: Two old colleagues still meet you for lunch. Neither mentions your last appraisals, though both read them.
Your name came off the circulation lists within a week. The lists did not notice.

scandal.text: Three former staff wrote to the newspaper in defence of {player.full} and {player.their} record. They knew it would not help.
In the building, "{player.given}" is still said carefully, like the name of a project that went wrong.

consultancy.text: Your old team still calls when something breaks. You never bill them for it.
Your old division still uses your templates. Your new firm bills them for it.

player.note: The start screen's choices, in the order shown, and what each one fills in. `label` is the choice as shown; `pool` is the cast.names pronoun a blank name is drawn from (default: the key); `honorific` goes before {player.formal} and {player.full}; every other field is a token, {player.<field>}, so a new choice or a new field is a data change (no field may be called name, given, formal or full: those are the name's forms, read from the one name field by `names`). Text only: nothing else in the game reads it. See docs/DESIGN.md section 7 and docs/CONTENT_PLAN.md section 8.

names.note: How a typed name is read into its three forms: {player.given} (what colleagues call you), {player.formal} (the honorific and the surname, or the given name where there is no surname) and {player.full} (the honorific and the whole name). A drawn name, or a typed one in cast.names, uses the pool's own given and formal. Matching ignores case. chineseSurnames: a name that starts with one is surname first ("Lim Wei Ling"), in Hanyu Pinyin and dialect spellings. chineseGiven: syllables of Chinese given names, so "Jia Hui" or "Kok Leong" typed alone has no surname, and "Siew Ling Tan" is read with the surname last. surnames: other surnames, which come last ("Prakash Pillai", "Joanne Pereira"); any unlisted last word is read as a surname too. fatherNames: a last word that is a father's name, not a surname ("Kavya Rajan": Ms Kavya). patronymics: bin, binte, s/o, d/o: the father's name follows, and there is no surname. surnameParticles: start a surname of two words ("Marcus de Souza"). noSurname: a first word that marks a Malay name with no surname even without bin ("Nurul Huda"). dropFromGiven: left off when colleagues say the given name ("Muhammad Faizal": Faizal). See docs/CONTENT_PLAN.md section 8; test/harness.test.js reads a table of sample names.

cast.note: The run's recurring people. See docs/CONTENT_PLAN.md section 8 for how cards use them. Names are invented; never add a real public figure, or a batchmate's name (rival.json).

A new face on your floor: {name}, who joined the service the year you did and has been, until now, a name on a cc line.

{name}, the first officer ever to report to you, is {aTitle}. You write performance objectives for someone else for the first time, and they are better than any you were given.
{name}, your first direct report, is {aTitle}, and calls you "{player.given}" on day one and "{player.formal}" on day two, after somebody has a word.

{name}, who reports to you, retires as {title}, after more years in the service than you have had. You speak at the farewell, and keep to time, as {name} always did.
{name}, who reports to you, retires as {title} and leaves a handover note that answers every question you were about to ask.

{name}, your new reporting officer, is {aTitle}, and sends a first all-staff email two lines long. The division finds this unsettling.

witnesses.note: Hidden witnesses (engine.js, 'hidden witnesses'). A card lists who could plausibly know what the player did there (its witnesses field, by: each witness type's chance of noticing, its reaction to each choice in appraisal points, and optionally a rare raise of the ceiling). Each type belongs to a ladder (ladder: service, the default, or politics): it sees only what the player does on that ladder, and its judgement lapses if the player is on the other ladder when it falls due. A witness who notices moves one appraisal one to three years later (delay), several in one year are capped (cap), and no single reaction is bigger than maxStep, so one witness nudges a grade and never jumps two. When a witness moves a grade, the review page shows one of its review lines about half the time (show), and the review's why line is left as it is. Nothing else is ever said: the ending never mentions witnesses. Player-facing text never says who: no names, titles or role words, and in politics no "upstairs" or "the building" (test/contexts.js checks). about and values are for writers only.

countersigner.about: The officer who countersigns your appraisal: your reporting officer's own boss. Reads your file every year and hears how things went, and you rarely meet.
countersigner.values: Judgement and steady delivery. Dislikes coasting, and spin that later unravels.

Between the draft and the final version, your appraisal gained a phrase: "a steady pair of hands". Nobody says who added it.
The comments section is a paragraph longer than the draft you were shown, and the new paragraph praises your judgement. It isn't signed.
Your grade came back higher than the draft you were shown. Nobody explains the difference, and you decide not to ask.
hurt: Your appraisal comes back with one sentence added under the grade: "Would benefit from greater consistency." It's in handwriting you don't recognise.
Between the draft and the final version, your appraisal lost the word "reliable". Nobody tells you who took it out.
Your grade came back lower than the draft you were shown. Nobody explains the difference, and the form has no box for asking.
The comments section now includes the phrase "not yet ready for more". It wasn't in the draft, and nobody says when it was added.

owner.about: The office a confidential paper or decision belongs to: the sender of the email, the owner of the plan. Knows exactly who was on the list, and sees what happens to its information.

help: The comments section mentions your discretion. Nobody tells you who raised it.
Your appraisal says you "can be trusted with sensitive material". You can't remember anyone watching you handle any.
Somebody asked for you by name this year, for work that was confidential. Nobody says why you.
hurt: The comments section uses the word "discretion" once, in a sentence that begins "Would benefit from". Nobody says whose sentence it is.
You were taken off the mailing list for confidential papers this year. Nobody tells you why, or who decided.
Your appraisal says you should "take more care with information". Nobody explains which information.

panel.about: The ranking panel: the directors who meet once a year to rank everyone at your grade, most of whom know you only by name. They go on what reaches them: names on papers, faces at meetings, stories.

help: When the grades were decided this year, somebody already knew your name, and that turned out to be enough.
Your appraisal mentions your "visible initiative". You hadn't thought anyone was looking.
Somebody you've never spoken to described you this year as "one to watch". It reached your file.
You hear, third-hand, that your name was mentioned this year as someone who gets things moving. Nobody says by whom.
hurt: When the grades were decided this year, your name came up attached to a story. Nobody tells you which one.
Your appraisal says you "could show more initiative". It's the only sentence that wasn't in last year's.
You hear, third-hand, that your name drew a pause this year when the grades were decided. Nobody tells you what the pause was about.

floor.about: The people who work around you: officers at your level and below, and the junior outside your door. Their anonymous feedback goes into your appraisal.
floor.values: Fairness to the people around you: who shares the credit, who covers, who leaves others to pick up the work.

help: This year's anonymous feedback from the people around you includes one comment that is just the word "fair". Nobody signs these, which is the point.
One anonymous comment this year calls you "the person you go to when it's gone wrong". You read it twice.
The anonymous feedback from the people around you is warmer than usual this year. You can't tell whose it is, and you aren't meant to.
An anonymous comment says you "share the credit and keep the blame". It isn't signed. None of them are.
hurt: One of this year's anonymous comments says you "take the credit and share the work". It isn't signed. None of them are.
This year's anonymous feedback has one sentence in it that nobody would say to your face. Somebody wrote it down anyway.
One anonymous comment this year is four words long: "Not a team player." You read it more often than you'd like.
The anonymous feedback from the people around you is cooler this year. Nobody says anything to your face, which is how you know.

ministersOffice.about: The Minister's office: the private secretaries and the press secretary who sit with the Minister, take notes in every room, and remember names.
ministersOffice.values: Being told the truth early, and no surprises. The two do not always agree.

help: This year your name was mentioned in a room you've never been in, as someone worth listening to. You find out only from the grade.
Somebody asked this year for "someone sensible" for a difficult job, and your name was the one given. You never find out who asked.
You hear, from nobody in particular, that you're thought of upstairs as "sound". In this building it's high praise.
hurt: Your name came up this year in a room you've never been in, next to the word "surprise". Nobody tells you which one.
Somewhere you've never been, this year, somebody asked who was responsible for an awkward moment. Your name was the answer.
You hear, from nobody in particular, that you're thought of upstairs as "not quite ready". Nobody says for what.

agencies.about: People from other agencies who were in the room or on the email. They talk to your directors at every inter-agency meeting.
agencies.values: Straight dealing: being told the truth, and not having their time wasted.

help: Somebody mentioned you this year, unprompted, as someone who plays it straight. It reached your file, and nobody tells you how.
An email you weren't copied on this year described you as "straight with us". It reached your file anyway.
Your appraisal says you are "trusted well beyond the division". Nobody says by whom.
hurt: Somebody mentioned your name this year at a meeting you weren't at. It didn't help, and nobody tells you what was said.
An email you weren't copied on this year asked for "someone else, if possible". Nobody tells you it was about you, but the grade does.
Your appraisal mentions "managing relationships" as an area to work on. Nobody says which relationships.

leadership.about: The party's leadership and the Prime Minister's office: the few people who decide who goes up, and who read everything that reaches them about you.
leadership.values: Loyalty in public, sound judgement in office, and nothing that embarrasses the government. Rewards a safe pair of hands; dislikes surprises and disagreement aired where the newspapers can see it.

help: Your name came up this year on a list you didn't know existed, among people thought ready for more. You find out only from the grade.
Somebody asked this year for "someone who won't need watching", and your name was the one given. Nobody tells you who asked.
You hear, from nobody in particular, that you're thought of as "safe" by the people whose opinion settles things. You decide to take it as praise.
A place was found for you this year at a dinner you hadn't expected to be asked to. Nobody says who found it.
hurt: Somebody used the word "unhelpful" this year, in a conversation about you that you weren't part of. Nobody tells you what it was about.
You hear, at second hand, that you're thought of this year as "one to watch". From the tone, it's the other kind.
A list went round this year of people ready for more. You hear about it only because your name wasn't on it.
The dinner you were asked to last year doesn't ask you this year. Nobody says why, and the menu was the same.

whips.about: The Whip's office: keeps the party's Members voting together, counts who turns up, and remembers who made its week harder.
whips.values: Discipline: turning up, voting with the party, and disagreeing in private. Rewards the reliable; dislikes surprises in public and anyone who freelances.

help: This year your name was ticked on a list kept somewhere you've never seen, under the heading "reliable". Nobody tells you, but the grade does.
You hear, from nobody in particular, that you're thought of as "no trouble at all". Coming from where it does, it's high praise.
A message this year thanked you, in three words, for something you don't remember doing. The grade suggests somebody remembers.
hurt: Your name was added this year to a short list kept somewhere you've never seen. Nobody says what the list is for.
You hear, from nobody in particular, that you've been described as "a free spirit". Nobody who said it meant it kindly.
The messages you get this year are a word shorter than last year's. You notice, and suspect you were meant to.

branch.about: Your party branch and its volunteers: the people who run your ward's Tuesday nights, walk the blocks with you and give their weekends to the party. What they think of you travels upwards.
branch.values: Showing up for the ward, and for them: staying late, sharing the credit, never leaving them to face residents alone. Dislikes an absent Member and a borrowed success.

help: More people turn up to help on Saturday mornings this year than last. Nobody says why, and you don't ask.
Somebody has started saving you a seat at the coffee shop on Tuesday nights. Nobody mentions it, which is how you know it means something.
What reaches the people who count about your ward this year is warmer than you'd have guessed. You can't tell who passed it on.
Somebody described you this year, at a meeting you weren't at, as "one of ours". It got back to you, and to everyone else.
hurt: Fewer people turn up to help on Saturday mornings this year. Nobody says why, which is how you know.
Somebody described you this year, at a meeting you weren't at, as "hard to find on a Tuesday". It travelled further than you'd like.
The seat at the coffee shop that used to be saved for you on Tuesday nights quietly stops being saved. Nobody says anything.
What reaches the people who count about your ward this year is cooler than you'd hoped. Nobody signs it.

pressGallery.about: The press gallery: the reporters who cover Parliament and your ministry, watch every answer, and decide which line becomes the story. The people who decide read them.
pressGallery.values: Candour and a straight answer. Rewards the quotable truth; punishes the evasion, the stonewall and the spin they can see through.

help: A Sunday column this year calls you "refreshingly straight". It's clipped and passed around by people you'll never meet.
A profile you didn't know was being written appeared this year. It's kinder than you'd have written yourself.
Your name turns up this year on a list of people "worth listening to". You find out because three people send it to you.
hurt: A Sunday column this year uses your name in a sentence about "answers that answer nothing". It's clipped and passed around.
A profile you didn't know was being written appeared this year. You read it twice, and then stop reading things.
Your name turns up this year on a list of people "who would rather not be asked". You find out because three people send it to you.

officials.about: The civil servants who work with you: your ministry's officials once you hold office, and the agencies that answer your letters and questions. From time to time they are asked for a frank view of the politicians they work with.
officials.values: Being listened to, being backed in public, and decisions made on evidence. Dislikes a politician who blames them, ignores them, or promises a date they then have to make true.

help: A frank view of you went in somewhere this year, from people who work with you every day. You never see it, and it helps.
The papers that reach you this year are noticeably better, and arrive a day earlier. Nobody says why, and you don't ask.
You hear, at second hand, that you're known as "someone who reads the annex". Where you heard it, that's the highest praise.
hurt: A frank view of you went in somewhere this year, from people who work with you every day. You never see it, and it doesn't help.
The papers that reach you this year are correct, complete and a day later than they used to be. Nobody says why.
You hear, at second hand, that you're known as "a reader of the summary". Nobody says who started it.

fellowMPs.about: Your fellow Members of Parliament: your GRC team, the Member for the next ward, the ministers across the table. They talk to each other, and to the people who decide.
fellowMPs.values: Collegiality: who shares the credit and the hard jobs, who covers for a colleague, and who grandstands or poaches at someone else's expense.

help: Somebody said, at a lunch you weren't at, that you're "good to have on the team". It reached the people who count.
You hear, third-hand, that your name was mentioned this year as someone who "makes the rest of us look good". Nobody says by whom.
A seat was kept for you this year at a table where you hadn't been asked to sit before. Nobody says who kept it.
hurt: Somebody said, at a lunch you weren't at, that you're "always in the photograph". It reached the people who count.
You hear, third-hand, that your name drew a sigh this year when it came up. Nobody tells you what the sigh was about.
The jokes about you this year have an edge they didn't used to have. Nobody says whose jokes they are.

warnLines: Your reporting officer asks whether you have considered the private sector. It is phrased as concern.
HR sends you a link to the career transition portal, "in case it is useful".
Your reporting officer mentions, twice, that a friend at a bank is hiring. It is phrased as news.
A workshop called "Planning Your Next Chapter" appears in your calendar, booked by someone else.
Your reporting officer says the service is "not for everyone", while looking just past your shoulder.
HR invites you to a briefing on "options outside the service". You are the only person invited.
Your reporting officer forwards you a job advertisement from a company in Jurong, with no message at all.
Someone from HR stops by your desk to ask how you are, really. It is the "really" that worries you.
warnLinesPolitics: The Whip asks, kindly, whether you have thought about spending more time in your ward. It is phrased as concern.
The Whip mentions several former Members who found fulfilling careers outside politics. It is phrased as an anecdote.
The party's organising secretary asks about your plans for the next election. It is years away.
Your seat on a committee you liked is given to a newer Member, with thanks for your contribution.
The Whip suggests you take on less committee work next year, "to focus". Nobody says on what.
The party asks you to help mentor a new face in your ward, "in case of anything". Nothing is the matter, you are told.

endgame.note: The end of a career, and what comes before it. See engine.js, 'the end of a career'. Retirement from the service at retireAge (64, from 1 July 2026); in politics the party asks Members not to stand at the first general election after renewalAge, unless stayOn holds (then politicalRetireAge, 70, is the stop for everyone). A Prime Minister serves a short tenure of cards (pmTenure: three or four, as many as fit before 70; the top job is not given without room for three). yearsInGrade sets the political ladder's pace (20 years from MP to Prime Minister, was 26), so careers peak at believable ages inside these limits. Lines are taken in an order drawn from the seed and never repeated in a run (headsUp lines cycle).

service: HR sends the pre-retirement briefing pack. You retire at {retire}, two years from now, and the pack has a page on it: the monthly payouts from your CPF, the retirement savings you have paid into since your first payslip, start at 65, a year later, and the page calls the year in between "a transition".

HR books you on the pre-retirement workshop, two years before you retire at {retire}. The first session asks everyone to list their hobbies. Most of the room lists projects they are still waiting to see finished.

The succession plan for your post is due, and this year it has your retirement date on it: two years from now, at {retire}. The form asks you to name two possible successors, and gives you three lines.
HR asks you to confirm your retirement date, two years away, at {retire}. You check it twice and send it back the same day, the first form in years you have not left for the end of the week.
Next year is your last before you retire. HR has started on your successor: the shortlist has three names on it, and you trained two of them.
Next year is your last. Your post is in the next posting exercise, and its job description has been rewritten for the first time since you wrote it.
Next year is your last. The new organisation chart already shows your post with a dotted line, which is how HR draws a job that is about to change hands.
Next year is your last. Someone has already booked the private room for your farewell lunch, a year ahead, because the good room goes fast in December.
renewal: The party has started talking about renewal before the next general election: new candidates, and older Members making way for them. Nobody says anything about it to you, and everybody is very warm.

The party has attached a younger activist to your campaign team ahead of the next general election. The activist sits in on your weekly sessions with residents and takes careful notes on the ward, as if expecting to need them.
At the party's year-end dinner the talk is of renewal before the next general election. You are seated with the Members first elected the year you were, and all of them are being very cheerful.
The Whip asks every Member to fill in a form on their "availability for the next term". You have never been asked this before. The form has two boxes.
Your volunteers now bring the party's new candidate to every event, standing one step behind you. By the end of the year the candidate is standing one step in front.
The volunteers at your weekly sessions with residents ask, carefully, whether they should stay on with the new candidate. You tell them yes. Most of them had already decided to.
The party introduces its new candidates in batches. The one for your ward is in the third batch, and the press release thanks you in its first paragraph.
The Whip's office collects every Member's diary for next year. Yours is blank from the start of the next campaign, and nobody asks why.
limit: You turn {limit} two years from now. The Prime Minister has said in Cabinet, to the table in general, that {limit} is where the party draws the line, and the table in general looked at you.
At the Cabinet retreat the group photograph is arranged by seniority, then again by age. You are at the same end both times, two years short of {limit}, the party's limit.
The Prime Minister's office asks every Minister for a portfolio note "for continuity". Yours is the only one with a date on it: two years from now, when you turn {limit}.
Two years before you turn {limit}, the party's limit, your press secretary starts a file called "Legacy". You find it by accident. It is very well organised.
Next year is your last in office. The reshuffle for when you turn {limit} has already been drafted, and you have been asked, kindly, for your comments on it.
Next year is your last. Your ministry has started copying your likely successor on everything, including, by accident, the email planning your farewell.
Next year is your last in Cabinet. Your office asks, as it asks every departing Minister, which of your papers you would like to keep. It is fewer than you expected.
Next year is your last. Your grassroots leaders are collecting for a farewell gift in secret, which in a ward this size means everyone has asked you what you would like.

service.first: Next year you'll have served long enough in your grade to be put up for {next} at the ranking, the yearly meeting where your bosses rank officers of the same grade against each other for promotion. Next year's appraisal will count.
blocked: Next year you'll have served long enough in your grade for {next}, but your name is not on the list for the ranking, the yearly meeting that decides promotions. Nobody says why.

By next year you'll have the years in your grade for {next}. The list for the ranking, the yearly meeting where promotions are decided, goes round without your name on it, and nobody mentions the gap.
Next year you'll be eligible for {next} on years served, but HR's list for the ranking, the yearly meeting that decides promotions, does not include you. You ask once. The answer is "not this cycle".

Your years in the grade will be enough for {next} next year, but your name will not go before the ranking, the yearly meeting that decides promotions. The explanation you get is a list of other people's strengths.
Next year you'll qualify for {next} on time served, and still not be put up at the ranking, the yearly meeting that decides promotions. HR calls it "a question of fit", without saying fit for what.
lines: Your name goes forward at next year's ranking, for {next}.
Next year's ranking will consider you for {next}, and next year's grade will be in front of it.
Your file goes to next year's ranking panel, for {next}.
Next year you're up for {next} at the ranking. It would help to have a good year.
Next year your name is on the ranking list for {next}. The list is confidential, so everyone on it behaves very well.
Next year the ranking considers you for {next}. People you have never worked with start copying you in on things, to see what you do with them.
Your file is in next year's ranking, for {next}, and someone has been asked to write a paragraph about you.
HR asks you to update your career summary before next year's ranking, where you will be considered for {next}. The form has a box for "key achievements", and a word limit.

politics.first: Your name goes forward for {next} at the Prime Minister's next reshuffle, when ministers and office holders are moved between jobs: by then you'll have served long enough. The year ahead will count.
blocked: Next year you'll have served long enough to be considered for {next}, but your name is not in the papers for the reshuffle, when the Prime Minister moves ministers and office holders between jobs. Nobody gives a reason.

You'll have served long enough for {next} by next year's reshuffle, when the Prime Minister moves ministers and office holders between jobs, but the shortlist the newspapers print leaves you off it. Nobody contradicts the newspapers.

By next year you'll have the time in office for {next}, but at the reshuffle, when the Prime Minister moves ministers and office holders between jobs, you are expected to "continue your good work" where you are.

Next year you'll be due for {next} on time served, but the reshuffle, when the Prime Minister moves ministers and office holders between jobs, is being planned without you. You can tell from how warmly everyone greets you.

You'll have served long enough for {next} by next year, but the reshuffle, when the Prime Minister moves ministers and office holders between jobs, will leave you where you are. The party calls you "invaluable in your present role".
politics.blockedPm: Next year you'll have served long enough to be weighed for the top job, but yours is not among the names being weighed. Nobody explains, and you do not ask.
politics.pm: Next year the party could choose you as its next leader, and so Prime Minister. It will be watching the year closely.
lines: Your name is on the list for next year's reshuffle, for {next}.
Next year's reshuffle will consider you for {next}, and next year's grade will be in front of it.
The party's Whip, who keeps its Members in line, mentions that your name is in the papers for next year's reshuffle, for {next}.
Next year you're in line for {next}, if the year goes well.
Next year's reshuffle will look at you for {next}. Your volunteers have heard, somehow, and are already saying "when", not "if".
The Prime Minister's Office asks for an updated résumé before next year's reshuffle, in which you are being considered for {next}. It asks politely, and twice.
Next year you are in the running for {next}. A senior minister you have barely spoken to invites you to lunch, and asks no questions at all, which is the question.
You are being considered for {next} at next year's reshuffle. The party's research staff ask for a list of your speeches, "for the file".

warnLate.service: A D is a formal warning, but next year is your last before you retire, and HR does not start an improvement plan in an officer's last year. The D stays on your file.
warnLate.slate: A D is a formal warning. Next year the party settles its slate of candidates for the coming general election, and this will be on the table when it does.
warnLate.leaving: A D is a formal warning, but next year is your last in office, and nobody is put on notice in their last year. The D stays on the record.

endgame.pmTooLate: The party will choose its next leader soon, and wants one with more than a year or two before 70. You are thanked, at length, for your willingness.

lines.tookOffice: You are sworn in at the Istana, the President's official residence. In your first speech you say you will serve a few years and then hand over, and every newspaper prints that sentence in a box.
teaNear: At a community event, a party activist asks for your card, and keeps it. In your experience, people do not keep cards.
Someone you have never met asks your office for a copy of your CV, "for a newsletter". There is no newsletter.
Your name appears on the guest list for a dinner where most of the other guests are Members of Parliament. Nobody tells you why you were asked.
A Member of Parliament from the party, whom you met once at a community event, sends a handwritten note: it was good to hear your remarks. You made no remarks.
seatAtRisk: The party's seat assessment for next year's general election lists your ward as "competitive". It is not a compliment.
Your volunteers' own canvass for next year's election comes back closer than last time, and their chairman has started saying "we" instead of "you".
Party headquarters sends extra volunteers to your ward a year before the election. It only does that for the wards it is worried about.
The party's own polling for next year's general election has your ward "in play". The phrase is new to you, and you do not like it.
With next year's general election a year away, your ward is on a list at party headquarters headed "Attention". You had hoped for a different list.
A newer Member from the next ward offers to lend you volunteers for next year's general election. The offer is kind, and tells you everything.
Your volunteers' chairman asks for a meeting about next year's general election, and brings a spreadsheet. Nobody brings a spreadsheet to a safe seat.
The coffee shop uncles in your ward have started discussing next year's general election in front of you, as if you were not there. Last time, they discussed it as if you had already won.
lines.pmFirstYear: There is no appraisal for a Prime Minister, only the newspapers every morning and Parliament on sitting days.
lines.pmLastYear: Your office starts boxing your papers for the National Archives. The boxes are numbered, and there are more of them than you expected.
pmElection: The general election falls in your tenure. The party is returned with a clear majority, and the commentary spends a week deciding whether the win was yours or the party's.
Polling Day comes round while you are Prime Minister. The party is returned, and your own ward's result is the first read out on television, which your volunteers take personally.
A general election comes due while you are Prime Minister, and the party is returned. On the night you speak from a school hall in your own ward, where the ceiling fans are louder than the cheering.
pmYears: Your diary for next year arrives already full. The one empty afternoon is marked "hold" by someone who is not you.
Your security officers know your routine better than you do, and have opinions about the hawker centre you stop at on Saturdays.
Cabinet meets every week. The colleagues who will be in the next Cabinet have started arriving early.

declassifiedFlags.label: Your last year
declassifiedFlags.text: Your handover file became the division's template for handover files. The template still has your mobile number in it.

declassifiedFlags.label: Your last year
declassifiedFlags.text: The change you pushed through in your last year is still running. The two colleagues who opposed it now describe it as theirs.

declassifiedFlags.label: Your last year
declassifiedFlags.text: Your desk emptied a box a week and nobody noticed. Your successor kept the stapler, without knowing it was there before you.

declassifiedFlags.label: Your last year
declassifiedFlags.text: Your successor kept your notes on the ward, and still calls the residents on your list first when a lift breaks down.

declassifiedFlags.label: Your last year
declassifiedFlags.text: Your last change became law just before you left. The Minister's speech in Parliament thanked the officers who drafted it, and not you, correctly.

declassifiedFlags.label: Your last year
declassifiedFlags.text: You handed over a case a week. Your volunteers held the dinner you were not supposed to know about. The speeches were the only surprise.

declassifiedFlags.label: The slate
declassifiedFlags.text: Asked to stay past 65, you stayed, to 70. The Prime Minister's note asking you is in your file. It is two lines long and says "no pressure" in both.

declassifiedFlags.label: The slate
declassifiedFlags.text: Asked to stay, you made way anyway. The candidate who took your place on the slate was never told you had been asked, and the Prime Minister has never said.

declassifiedFlags.label: The slate
declassifiedFlags.text: You asked to stand once more. The Whip's note of the meeting is one line long, and leaves out the answer, because everyone knew it.

declassifiedFlags.label: The slate
declassifiedFlags.text: The candidate you walked round every block won the ward with a bigger swing than you ever had, and thanked you first.

declassifiedFlags.label: The slate
declassifiedFlags.text: Your statement said you had decided to make way. The Whip kept a copy, as an example for the next Members asked.

declassifiedFlags.label: The succession
declassifiedFlags.text: The younger ministers chose, one private conversation at a time, and you were not consulted. Every one of them now says the choice was obvious.

declassifiedFlags.label: The succession
declassifiedFlags.text: You chose your successor yourself. The history books say so in one sentence, and then move on to your successor.

declassifiedFlags.label: The succession
declassifiedFlags.text: You kept the succession open for a year. All three contenders later called it the hardest year of their careers, and the most productive.

declassifiedFlags.label: Afterwards
declassifiedFlags.text: Senior Minister: a title, a seat in Cabinet and the office down the corridor. You gave your view only when asked, which was more often than you expected.

declassifiedFlags.label: Afterwards
declassifiedFlags.text: No title. Tuesday nights at Meet-the-People Sessions until the next election. The first resident in the queue had a parking fine, and it was waived, on appeal, through the proper channels.

declassifiedFlags.label: Afterwards
declassifiedFlags.text: Your successor's first year had no surprises in it. The evenings you spent going through the files together are why.

lines: That's three Cs in a row, so HR moves you sideways: the same grade, in another division. It's meant as a fresh start. Nobody there asked for you, but the work is real.
Three Cs in a row means a move, and HR has found you one: the same grade, a different division, and a desk by the window that nobody else wanted.
After three Cs in a row, HR moves you sideways, to another division at your grade. The transfer letter calls it "a development opportunity", in bold.
That makes three Cs in a row, and the service's answer is a sideways move: another division, the same grade, and a welcome email with your name spelt wrong.
Three Cs in a row, so you are moved sideways to another division, at the same grade. Your new colleagues are kind, and have clearly been briefed.
HR's rule after three Cs in a row is a fresh start, so you move sideways: another division, the same grade, and a handover file from someone who left in a hurry.
Three Cs in a row: HR moves you to another division at your grade, "to see you in a different light". The light is fluorescent, as before.
After a third C in a row you are posted sideways, to a division at the same grade that is short of people. Short enough that nobody asks why you came.
sideways.named: From next year your papers go to a new reporting officer instead of {senior}.

folder.thin: The folder on the table is thin. The person reading it seems, very slightly, disappointed.
folder.nothing: There is nothing to disclose. Your interviewer closes the folder, which takes no time at all.
disclosed: You disclose {item}. The interviewer writes something down.
You disclose {item}. The interviewer turns a page, and keeps a finger on it.
You disclose {item}. There is a pause, long enough to count in.
You disclose {item}. The interviewer nods, as if it were already known, which it may have been.
You disclose {item}. The note-taker stops writing, then starts again.
You disclose {item}. The interviewer thanks you for it, which is not the same as being glad.
You disclose {item}. The interviewer underlines something on a page you cannot see.
folder.found: {item}: on day four of the campaign, someone has found it.

threeCsPolitics: That's three Cs in a row, so the Whip moves you to chair a parliamentary committee nobody wanted to sit on. The work is real, at least.
That's three Cs in a row, so the Whip finds you a new responsibility: a parliamentary committee whose last report is older than some of its members. Nobody else wanted it, which is why it is yours.
That's three Cs in a row, so the Whip moves you onto a parliamentary committee that meets on Friday afternoons. It has a great deal of work and no audience at all.
That's three Cs in a row, so the Whip asks you to lead a parliamentary committee on a subject nobody can explain in one sentence. Eventually, you can.
